gloss: The iconic opening cadence of Ulysses. Based closely on Oliver St. John Gogarty (1878–1957), Dublin physician, poet, and athlete. 'Stately' parodies priestly dignity and epic gravity; 'Buck' evokes eighteenth-century Regency dandyism, hedonism, and impudent bravura.

lemma: a mirror and a razor lay crossed
quote: a mirror and a razor lay crossed
gloss: Mulligan's shaving instruments prefigure the liturgical trappings of a Catholic priest preparing for Mass. Crossed, they form the crux decussata (St. Andrew's cross) and evoke Oscar Wilde's preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray: 'The nineteenth century dislike of Realism is the rage of Caliban seeing his own face in a glass.'

Latin: 'I will go in unto the altar of God.' The traditional opening versicle of the Tridentine Catholic Mass (Psalm 42:4 in the Vulgate). Spoken at the foot of the altar, Mulligan uses it here to inaugurate a mock-blessing over Dublin Bay and Sandycove from the top of the Martello Tower.
scholars: The Roman Missal (Tridentine Rite), Judica me, Deus

gloss: Greek: 'Golden-mouthed' (χρυσόστομος). An epithet originally applied to Dio Chrysostom and later to St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople, celebrated for his eloquence and denunciation of clerical luxury. Stephen ironically reflects on Mulligan's gold-capped teeth and caustic, irreverent tongue.

The circular granite firing platform atop the Sandycove Martello Tower (Tower No. 11, built 1804 by the British Board of Ordnance). It served as an emplacement for a rotating 24-pounder cannon facing out across Dublin Bay. In 1904, Gogarty leased it from the War Office for £8 a year.

lemma: The snotgreen sea. The scrotumtightening sea.
quote: The snotgreen sea. The scrotumtightening sea.
gloss: Mulligan's notorious compound epithets. Parodies classical Homeric formulas ('wine-dark sea', epi oinopa ponton) through visceral bodily realism and mock-medical vernacular. Also alludes to the emerald green flag of Irish nationalism and the Greek sea god Proteus.

lemma: The rage of Caliban at not seeing his face in a glass
quote: The rage of Caliban at not seeing his face in a glass
gloss: Direct quotation from Oscar Wilde's preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891): 'The nineteenth century dislike of Romanticism is the rage of Caliban not seeing his own face in a glass.' Caliban represents the savage, colonized subject in Shakespeare's The Tempest; here Mulligan casts Stephen as the resentful, melancholic poet gazing into the cracked lookingglass of Ireland.

Stephen's stinging definition of Irish art under British and Vatican colonial subjugation. Synthesizes Wilde's aphorism with Swift's Preface to The Battle of the Books ('Satyr is a sort of Glass, wherein Beholders do generally discover every body's Face but their Own'). Establishes the domestic servant status of Ireland.

Ulysses opens and closes with the serpentine letter S. This has been compared to the figures of serpents in the Book of Kells that have their tails in their mouths (ouroboros): Ulysses is a closed circle, ending where it began. In Finnegans Wake Joyce achieved a similar effect by linking the opening and closing sentences of the book so that the former completes the latter.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: The three parts into which Joyce divides Ulysses open with significant letters:
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Latin hymn from the Ordo Commendationis Animae (the Catholic Roman Ritual for the Commendation of a Departing Soul): 'May the glittering throng of confessors, white as lilies, encompass thee.' Stephen prayed this at the deathbed of his mother May Dedalus (née Mary Joyce), an agony that haunts him throughout the entire day of June 16, 1904.
For all his cynicism and neo-paganism, Buck Mulligan is identified as an upholder of church and state.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (1) Fat, chubby. Joyce's principal model for Buck Mulligan, Oliver St. John Gogarty, was hardly plump. Ellmann writes that when Joyce first met Gogarty in the National Library in 1903, Gogarty was "handsome, lithe though inclined to fat, prosperous and merry."[4] In 1904 Gogarty attended Oxford, where, in his own words, he "became mentally and physically pinguis [Latin: fat]".[5] Whether plump is an accurate description of Gogarty, there is no doubt that Joyce intended Buck Mulligan to be fat: in Oxen of the Sun (384.33-36), Dixon jocosely inquires whether Mulligan's "incipient ventripotence" indicates that he is pregnant. It is possible that, in the Shakespearean context of Ulysses, Joyce intended Mulligan to represent the fat knight Falstaff to Stephen's Prince Hal.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (2) Blunt (in manners); crude; rude; clownish.[6] These adjectives accurately describe Mulligan's character.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Malachi Mulligan is a portrait of Oliver St. John Gogarty, a young writer and medical student with whom Joyce (portrayed here as Stephen Dedalus) lived for six nights (9-14 June 1904) in the Martello Tower at Sandycove. According to the two schemas which Joyce provided for Ulysses, Buck Mulligan here represents Antinous, the leader of the suitors of Penelope in the Odyssey. As Stephen represents Hamlet as well as the Odyssey's Telemachus, Mulligan can also be identified with Claudius.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: A stairhead is a level space at the top of a flight of steps. In the Martello tower at Sandycove, a narrow spiral staircase of stone steps leads from the interior of the tower to the roof or terreplein. Buck Mulligan, in mockery of the Catholic ceremony of the Mass, has just ascended these steps in imitation of a Catholic priest ascending the steps to the altar.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: A more solemn word than carrying. One also bears arms, appropriate here, as Mulligan and Stephen will cross swords in this episode. The military setting in the Martello tower underscores the sense or meaning Joyce assigned to this episode in the Linati schema: Il figlio spodestato alla lotta ("The dispossessed son in combat").
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Mulligan's shaving bowl represents the chalice that holds the wine, which becomes the blood of Christ in the Mass.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Middle English phrase: 'Again-bite of inner wit' (the remorse of conscience), from Dan Michel of Northgate's 1340 Kentish translation of Ayenbite of Inwyt (itself a translation of Friar Lorens' Somme le Roi). Serves as Stephen Dedalus's primary recurrent guilt motif over his refusal to kneel and pray at his dying mother's bedside.

The first of many allusions in this episode to blades and cutting. Mulligan is a shaver, and also a future surgeon, but the deadliest weapon in this episode is neither the razor nor the scalpel. Rather than belonging to Mulligan, it is in the possession of Stephen (at least as he sees it). It is the lancet of his (Stephen's) art, the cold steel pen. This allusion is a play on the phrase "the pen is mightier than the sword".
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (Latin) I will go in to the altar of God. The Latin Tridentine Mass opens with the Prayers at the Foot of the Altar. After making the Sign of the Cross, the priest and his servers intone an antiphon based on Psalm 43 (Vulgate 42), Iudica Me, Deus (Judge Me, O God), the fourth verse of which Mulligan quotes. By intoning these words after he has ascended the steps, Mulligan has perverted the order of the liturgy.[8]
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (Greek) Χρυσόστομος is Greek for golden-mouthed, a common epithet meaning eloquent, though here it refers literally to Mulligan's gold-pointed teeth.[10] The epithet was applied to St John Chrysostomos, one of the fathers of the Greek church, whose name recalls that of Oliver St John Gogarty, Joyce's principal model for Buck Mulligan. On 16 June, the feast of the confessor St John Francis Regis, the fourth lesson of the Second Nocturn would have been taken from one of John Chrysostom's sermons.[11]
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Stephen's silent, bitter epithet for Buck Mulligan at the conclusion of Episode 1. Directly links the episode to Homer's Odyssey, where Antinous and the insolent suitors usurp Telemachus's patrimony and feast in Odysseus's hall. Mulligan has taken Stephen's key and money, leaving Stephen dispossessed.

The two whistles represent the sacring bell, which is rung during the elevation of the consecrated Host during Mass. The origin of these helpful whistles is still a mystery. There are two obvious sources: (1) the mailboat, which is just about to leave Kingtown Harbour, about 1200 metres away (see 005.17) (2) a train arriving at Sandycove Railway Station, about 900 metres away.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: To raise a possible parallel with or echo of Cervantes, Roger B. Salomon[16] suggests Joyce in Portrait and Ulysses has Stephen play out the mock-heroic mode invented by Cervantes in Don Quixote, combining both nostalgic creator and ironic critic. (The mock hero aligns his deepest emotional attachments to dead mythologies and forgotten codes of ethics; an alienated figure in a landscape hostile to the possibility of any kind of attainment. The reader is witness to a dialogue between the real and a faded ideal, between the sensible and the admirable.) He suggests Buck Mulligan plays the part of both supportive friend and deflating realist a la Sancho Panza in Don Quixote. This role, though in a more kindly and distant way, seems to transfer to Leopold Bloom. This is just one thread in a myriad of literary allusions Joyce draws upon, but nevertheless a powerful one.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: symbolical of birth and the interconnectedness of all life; the seat of the soul and the point at which mystics stare while meditating. Stephen may be suggesting that contemporary Irish nationalism was little more than self-centred navel-gazing. See 038.11 ff.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: The Oracle of Delphi was believed to be located at the centre of the world, which was represented by a stone known as the omphalos.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (Middle English) Remorse of conscience.[1] Stephen has modernized the Middle English spelling Ayenbite of Inwyt. This is the title of a translation of a French moral treatise Le Somme de Vices et de Virtues (The Book of Vices and Vertues), written in 1279 by the Dominican monk Frère Lorens (Laurentius Gallus). Lorens was confessor to Philip III of France and it was for the king that he wrote the treatise. It is a layman's manual of sins and virtues, similar in content and style to The Parson's Tale in Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales. The English translation was made in 1340 by Dan Michel of Northgate, and is highly valued today by scholars of Middle English, being one of the few surviving works in the Kentish dialect.[2]
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

lemma: We have grown out of Wilde and paradoxes
quote: We have grown out of Wilde and paradoxes
gloss: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray, Chapter Two: "The few words that Basil's friend [Lord Henry Wotton] had said to him—words spoken by chance, no doubt, and with wilful paradox in them...."
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (French) Go to hell! Goddamn![1] Zut is a coarse exclamation signifying refusal or (as here) dismissal.[2] Nom de Dieu (literally, name of God) is a blasphemous oath signifying shock or indignation.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: A red-haired girl seen on Carlisle Pier in Kingstown (Dunleary).
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (German) literally Superman.[1] The Übermensch is a philosophical concept introduced by Thomas Carlyle in 1840 in his book On Heroes, Hero-Worship and the Heroic in History.[2] The book proposed that "The history of the world is but the biography of great men,"[3] and that each era of human civilization was defined by the abilities and religion of its Übermensch. Used this way, Joyce would be advocating that his heroes are the defining force behind their society.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: See 010.21-22. Stephen's emended version, laid out as a tercet, anticipates the tercet of Heighos at the end of Calypso. Presumably it is 8:45 am as Stephen sets off for Dalkey. For Bloom, the bells of St George's Church are tolling for Paddy Dignam; for Stephen, the bells (real or imaginary) are ringing for his mother.[1]
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: In grammar, the genitive or possessive case has several different forms. The Latin phrase Amor matris is ambiguous to Stephen because it means two different things depending on whether matris is subjective genitive or objective genitive:

gloss: A mother's love [for her child]
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: [A child's] love for his mother
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

lemma: — You, Cochrane, what city sent for him?
quote: — You, Cochrane, what city sent for him?
gloss: Opening line of Episode 2 (Nestor). Stephen Dedalus is teaching an ancient history lesson on Pyrrhus of Epirus at the Clifton School in Dalkey. The classroom setting establishes the episode's art (History) and catechistic technique.

lemma: Another victory like that and we are done for.
quote: Another victory like that and we are done for.
gloss: The classic definition of a Pyrrhic victory after the Battle of Asculum (279 BC). Stephen reflects on the futility of military triumphs, foreshadowing his upcoming discussion on the nightmare of history with the headmaster Mr. Deasy.
(Latin) By straight roads; By straight paths. This is the Blackwood family motto.[1] It is also the school motto of Belvedere College in Dublin, which Joyce attended from 1893 until 1898.[2]
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Henry Weysford Charles Plantagenet (1842–1868), was a British peer.[1] In the Irish peerage he held the titles Earl of Moira and Baron Rawdon of Moira, both of which became extinct upon his death. His racehorse Repulse won the 1000 Guineas Stakes at Newmarket in 1866 over a distance of 1 mile (1609 metres).[2] The winning jockey was Tom Cannon, Sr, a greatgrandfather of Lester Piggott.[3] The horse was trained by John Day, Jr. The 1000 Guineas is run by three-year old thoroughbred fillies.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Hugh Grosvenor (1825–1899) was a successful racehorse onwer and Master of the Horse from 1880-1885. His horse Shotover won the Epsom Derby in 1882 over a distance of 1½ miles (2414 metres).[4] The winning jockey was Tom Cannon, who had ridden Repulse to victory in the 1000 Guineas sixteen years earlier.[5] The horse was trained by John Porter. Shotover also won the 2000 Guineas Stakes in 1882 with the same jockey. The Epsom Derby and the 2000 Guineas are run by three-year old thoroughbreds.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

lemma: the duke of Beaufort's Ceylon, prix de Paris, 1866
quote: the duke of Beaufort's Ceylon, prix de Paris, 1866
gloss: (French) The Grand Prix de Paris is a French flat horse race for three-year old thoroughbreds.[6] Inaugurated in 1863, it is run every July at Longchamp Racecourse in Paris. In 1866 it was indeed won by Henry Somerset, 8th Duke of Beaufort's Ceylon over a distance of 3000 metres.[7] The winning jockey was once again Tom Cannon,[8] and the trainer John Day. Beaufort (1824–1899) was the Master of the Horse from 1858–1859 and from 1866-1868.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Presumably Repulse, Shotover and Ceylon are carrying the same rider: the jockey Tom Cannon, Sr, who rode them to victory in their Classic triumphs. Is Mr Deasy an admirer of Cannon?
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (German) women.[2] Originally the term was used when referring to women of the better classes, or ladies, but by the end of the 19th century it had acquired a pejorative meaning: wenches, drabs, slovens.

gloss: (Latin) eternal law. St Thomas Aquinas discusses the various kinds of law in his Summa Theologica. In the First Part of Part 2, Question 91, Article 1, he writes:

gloss: (Byzantine Greek) An omophorion is the distinctive vestment of a bishop in the Eastern Orthodox Church.[7] Originally made of wool or sheepskin, the omophorion now resembles a long broad scarf of white brocade decorated with four crosses and an eight-pointed star. It is worn about the neck and shoulders in such a manner that the ends cross on the left shoulder, one end falling to the knees in front, the other behind. As a presbyter, Arius would have been entitled to wear an omophorion.[8] In the Western Church, the omophorion evolved into the pallium.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: Duces tecum is Latin for bring with you. A writ of duces tecum, or a subpoena duces tecum, is a summons that requires a witness to bring specified documents when he or she appears in court to give testimony.[1]
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (Latin) May she rest.[2] Oscar Wilde wrote this short poem in memory of his sister Isola. Requiescat was written in Avignon in 1874, seven years after Isola died (23 February 1867, less than two months before her 10th birthday). It was included in the collection Rosa Mystica (1881). Wilde was twelve when Isola died and nineteen when he wrote the poem.
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (Italian) On guard! Be vigilant![3] These are the opening words of Giuseppe Verdi's opera Il Trovatore (The Troubador).
scholars: Wikibooks: Annotations to James Joyce's Ulysses (CC-BY-SA 4

gloss: (Italian) Sortita is a musical term for a principal singer's first entrance in an opera; an aria di sortita is the song the character sings when he makes his first appearance. Di due figli vivea (Of two sons there lived) is the aria di sortita of Ferrando, the Count of Luna's captain of the guard, in Verdi's Il Trovatore.[4] The aria is preceded by a recitative, which opens with the words All'erta! All'erta (On guard! On guard!).

But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him".

gloss: (Italian) O yes, certainly![7] In Italian the word for yes is usually spelt sì (or, rarely, sí). Sì certo, without the comma, means certainly.

gloss: (Sanskrit) This is an esoteric term used in Hinduism to denote a very long period of time.[1] A manvantara is a period of time equal to the lifespan of a Manu: 306,720,000 years. A mahamanvantara or mahakalpa is a period of time equal to the lifespan of Brahma: 311,040,000,000,000 years.

quote: Paysayennn. P. C. N., you know : physiques, chimiques et naturelles
gloss: (French) physical, chemical and natural.[14] Paysayenn is a phonetic spelling of how a Frenchman would pronounce the letters P. C. N. The letters are an abbreviation for the French phrase Physique-Chimie-Sciences naturelles (Physics, Chemistry, Natural Science). In December 1902, Joyce was granted a provisional card of admission to the course for the certificate in physics, chemistry and biology at the École de Médecine in Paris. This certificate was required before he would be permitted to study medicine. As it happened, his medical ambitions only lasted a few more days.[15] Note that Stephen's translation of P. C. N. is not quite correct.

gloss: (French) lung stew.[16] A stew made from the lungs or lights of butchered animals would have been one of the cheapest dishes available in a Paris restaurant.

gloss: (French slang) Boulevard Saint-Michel.[17] In 1904 the Boulevard Saint-Michel, a street on the Left Bank of the Seine in Paris, was the café centre of the city's student and bohemian life.

gloss: (French) I am he.[1] Stephen's statement is a parody of the oft-quoted remark attributed to Louis XIV of France: L'état, c'est moi (I am the state).

[I] must get [this money order cashed]. To which the usher replied: [We're] closed.

gloss: (French Slang) A small black coffee.[1] The usual French term for a small black coffee is demitasse. A sétier is an obsolete unit of capacity and volume. It was used before the French Revolution to express the capacity of dry substances, such as seeds and grains, and the volume of liquids. Its value varied from place to place, but the Parisian dry sétier was equal to 151.680 litres.[2] The liquid sétier was equivalent to about 9 litres, or to 284 millilitres, depending on the source consulted.[3] The latter would make a demi-sétier equal to about 142 ml, which is appropriate for a small cup of coffee.

lemma: Mr Leopold Bloom ate with relish the inner organs of beasts and fowls.
quote: Mr Leopold Bloom ate with relish the inner organs of beasts and fowls.
gloss: The iconic opening sentence of Part II (The Odyssey) and Episode 4 (Calypso), introducing Leopold Bloom at 8:00 AM in the kitchen of 7 Eccles Street. Immediately establishes Bloom's earthy, visceral, and sensuous humanity in contrast to Stephen Dedalus's scholastic asceticism.

lemma: grilled mutton kidneys which gave to his palate a fine tang of faintly scented urine
quote: grilled mutton kidneys which gave to his palate a fine tang of faintly scented urine
gloss: Key anatomical correspondence for Calypso: the Kidney (organ). Joyce foregrounds somatic biology and gastrointestinal reality, evoking Homer's epic feasts through the modest breakfast of a Dublin advertising canvasser.

lemma: By lorries along sir John Rogerson's quay Mr Bloom walked soberly
quote: By lorries along sir John Rogerson's quay Mr Bloom walked soberly
gloss: Opening of Episode 5 (Lotus Eaters). 10:00 AM. Leopold Bloom walks through the south docklands towards Westland Row, enveloped in the heavy atmosphere of narcotic ease, botanical languor, and colonial inertia corresponding to Homer's land of the Lotus-eaters.
Bloom's undercover epistolary pseudonym for his secret romantic correspondence with Martha Clifford. The flower motif reinforces the botanical and narcotic themes of the episode.

lemma: Martin Cunningham, first, pushed homely yellow chipped stone
quote: Martin Cunningham, first, pushed homely yellow chipped stone
gloss: Opening of Episode 6 (Hades). 11:00 AM. Leopold Bloom boards the funeral carriage at Sandymount for Paddy Dignam's burial at Prospect Cemetery in Glasnevin. The journey through Dublin represents Odysseus's nekyia (descent into the Underworld).

lemma: Martin Cunningham's face was like a block of carved limestone.
quote: Martin Cunningham's face was like a block of carved limestone.
gloss: Martin Cunningham represents Sisyphus in the Homeric scheme. His face resembles the limestone rock of Dublin, burdened by his tragic family life (an alcoholic wife), yet maintaining gentle Christian compassion.

lemma: IN THE HEART OF THE HIBERNIAN METROPOLIS
quote: IN THE HEART OF THE HIBERNIAN METROPOLIS
gloss: The celebrated opening headline of Episode 7 (Aeolus). 12:00 PM (Noon). Set in the newspaper offices of The Freeman's Journal and Evening Telegraph. Joyce introduces 63 newspaper headlines that mock imperial rhetoric, journalistic sensationalism, and the gusty winds of Dublin political speech.

Nelson's Pillar in O'Connell Street (then Sackville Street), the central tramway hub of Dublin. The monument to the British naval hero Horatio Nelson symbolizes imperial dominance over Dublin, later mocked in Stephen Dedalus's 'Parable of the Plums'.

lemma: Pineapple rock, lemon platt, butter scotch.
quote: Pineapple rock, lemon platt, butter scotch.
gloss: Opening cadence of Episode 8 (Lestrygonians). 1:00 PM. Leopold Bloom gazes into the confectioner's window of Graham Lemon on Sackville Street. The episode's organ is the Esophagus and its technique is Peristalsis, saturating the narrative with hunger, chewing, digestion, and predatory consumerism.

An evangelical throwaway flyer advertising the apocalyptic revival meetings of Dr. John Alexander Dowie. Bloom receives it and later casts it upon the River Liffey, where it bobs downstream towards Dublin Bay throughout the afternoon.

lemma: Urbane, to comfort them, the quaker librarian purred:
quote: Urbane, to comfort them, the quaker librarian purred:
gloss: Opening of Episode 9 (Scylla and Charybdis). 2:00 PM. Set in the National Library of Ireland on Kildare Street. Introduces Thomas William Lyster, the scholarly quaker librarian, engaging with George Russell (A.E.), John Eglinton, and Stephen Dedalus as Stephen prepares his dialectical Hamlet theory.

Stephen's celebrated theological-literary paradox: applying the Sabellian heresy and Trinitarian dogma to Shakespeare's ghost in Hamlet, arguing that the artist is the father of all his creations and his own spiritual progenitor.

lemma: The superior, the very reverend John Conmee S.J. reset his smooth watch in his pocket
quote: The superior, the very reverend John Conmee S.J. reset his smooth watch in his pocket
gloss: Opening of Episode 10 (Wandering Rocks). 3:00 PM. Father John Conmee, S.J., former rector of Clongowes Wood College, begins his afternoon walk through the north side of Dublin. The episode is structured in 19 synchronous mini-scenes weaving across the civic labyrinth of Dublin.

Joyce's Jesuit boarding school in County Kildare, prominently featured in A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. Conmee represents the spiritual authority of Rome in Ireland alongside the Viceroy's British imperial power.

lemma: Bronze by gold heard the hoofirons, steelyringing.
quote: Bronze by gold heard the hoofirons, steelyringing.
gloss: The famous polyphonic opening chord of Episode 11 (Sirens). 4:00 PM. Set in the Ormond Hotel bar on the Liffey quays. 'Bronze' represents the bronze-haired barmaid Lydia Douce; 'gold' represents Mina Kennedy. The first sixty lines form a musical overture announcing all acoustic themes developed across the episode.
Acoustic deformation of 'impertinent insolence', mimicking the rhythm and dissonance of musical notes sounding together in a fugue ('fuga per canonem').

lemma: I was just passing the time of day with old Troy of the D.M.P.
quote: I was just passing the time of day with old Troy of the D.M.P.
gloss: Opening of Episode 12 (Cyclops). 5:00 PM. Barney Kiernan's pub on Little Britain Street. Narrated by an unnamed Dublin debt-collector using cynical, vernacular Dublin slang, juxtaposed against 33 hyperbolic parodies written in heroic, Ossianic, legal, and biblical styles ('gigantism').

Modeled closely on Michael Cusack (1847–1906), founder of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA). The Citizen embodies militant, narrow, and anti-Semitic Irish chauvinism, acting as the one-eyed Cyclops (Polyphemus) who hurls a biscuit-tin at Bloom.

lemma: The summer evening had begun to fold the world in its mysterious embrace.
quote: The summer evening had begun to fold the world in its mysterious embrace.
gloss: Opening cadence of Episode 13 (Nausicaa). 8:00 PM. Sandymount Strand. Joyce adopts the sentimental, cliché-ridden prose of Victorian romantic magazines (The Lady's Pictorial) to narrate the inner fantasy world of Gerty MacDowell, who sits on the strand gazing across at Leopold Bloom.

Gerty represents Homer's Phaeacian princess Nausicaa, who discovers the shipwrecked Odysseus on the shore. Joyce pairs her youth and physical disability (a subtle limp) with the litany of the Virgin Mary sounding from the nearby Star of the Sea church.

lemma: Deshil Holles Eamus. Deshil Holles Eamus. Deshil Holles Eamus.
quote: Deshil Holles Eamus. Deshil Holles Eamus. Deshil Holles Eamus.
gloss: The incantatory opening of Episode 14 (Oxen of the Sun). 10:00 PM. Holles Street National Maternity Hospital. Fuses Irish 'deiseal' (sunwise, auspicious direction), Holles Street, and Latin 'eamus' ('Let us go sunwise to Holles Street'). Joyce constructs the episode as an exact chronological evolution of English prose style (from Latinate incantations and Old English alliteration to Carlyle and modern slang), mimicking the nine-month gestation of a human fetus.

lemma: Send us bright one, light one, Horhorn, quickening and wombfruit.
quote: Send us bright one, light one, Horhorn, quickening and wombfruit.
gloss: Invocation mimicking early medieval Anglo-Saxon alliterative verse. The organ is the Womb and the art is Medicine, tracking Mina Purefoy's protracted labor within the hospital while Stephen and medical students drink beer in the common room.

Opening stage direction of Episode 15 (Circe). 12:00 AM (Midnight). Dublin's red-light district (Nighttown / Monto), centered around Tyrone and Mabbot Streets. Structured entirely as an expressionist theatrical playscript where psychological repressions, hallucinations, and guilt figures materialize physically.
Joyce's term for the Monto brothel quarter of Dublin, at the time the largest red-light district in the British Isles. Corresponds to Circe's island of Aeaea where men are transformed into swine.

lemma: Preparatory to anything else Mr Bloom brushed off the dust from Stephen's clothes.
quote: Preparatory to anything else Mr Bloom brushed off the dust from Stephen's clothes.
gloss: Opening of Part III (The Nostos) and Episode 16 (Eumaeus). 1:00 AM. Leopold Bloom guides an exhausted, shaken Stephen Dedalus to the cabman's shelter under Loopline Bridge near Custom House Quay. Written in an intentionally fatigued, cliché-laden, and circumlocutory prose style reflecting somatic physical exhaustion.

James Fitzharris (1833–1910), nicknamed 'Skin-the-Goat', driver of the getaway cab in the 1882 Phoenix Park Murders of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Thomas Henry Burke. He runs the cabman's shelter, embodying unrepentant Fenian physical force nationalism.

lemma: What parallel courses did Bloom and Stephen follow returning?
quote: What parallel courses did Bloom and Stephen follow returning?
gloss: The famous opening question of Episode 17 (Ithaca). 2:00 AM. 7 Eccles Street. Joyce's favorite episode, composed entirely in impersonal, scientific catechism (questions and answers). Reduces the heroic homecoming of Odysseus and Telemachus to mathematical equations, astronomical coordinates, and physical laws.

lemma: the key of the front door was in the pocket of the other trousers
quote: the key of the front door was in the pocket of the other trousers
gloss: The comedic climax of the homecoming: Bloom has forgotten the latchkey of 7 Eccles Street in his morning trousers, mirroring Stephen's earlier dispossession of the Martello Tower key by Buck Mulligan in Episode 1.

lemma: Yes because he never did a thing like that before as ask to get his breakfast in bed
quote: Yes because he never did a thing like that before as ask to get his breakfast in bed
gloss: The triumphant opening phrase of Episode 18 (Penelope). The unpunctuated stream-of-consciousness monologue of Molly Bloom lying in bed at 7 Eccles Street beside her sleeping husband. Composed of eight unpunctuated giant paragraphs, beginning with the primordial affirmation 'Yes' and ending with the ecstatic embrace on Howth Head.

Howth Head, the dramatic promontory overlooking Dublin Bay where Leopold proposed to Molly among the rhododendrons sixteen years earlier in 1888. The geography anchors both Ulysses and Finnegans Wake (Howth Castle and Environs).
